newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. said eager to break China-WTO impasse.
newsitem.headline: U.S. said eager to break China-WTO impasse.

text.p: The United States is eager to break an impasse over China's entry into the World Trade Organisation (WTO) and has been quietly working to close gaps before talks in Geneva, a former U.S. official said on Friday.

Harald Malmgren, deputy U.S. trade representative under former U.S. Presidents Richard Nixon and Gerald Ford, said the recent appointment of Lee Sands as U.S. negotiator on China's WTO bid was aimed at infusing new impetus into the talks, Kyodo news agency reported.
"This was not a decision by trade officials, this came from the top... My impression is he (U.S. President Bill Clinton) says 'Let's move things ahead', " Malmgren said.

Malmgren said Clinton had decided to act because of confidence that he would win next month's presidential election and because momentum within China for more free-market reforms to meet WTO requirements was diminishing.

"He hasn't been clear in public...and the president will, of course, not say anything before the election," Kyodo quoted Malmgren as saying, pointing to strong opposition from labour unions, human rights advocates and environmentalists against a speedy admission of China into the global trade body.
"(The Office of) the U.S. Trade Representative has in the last three weeks engaged the Chinese side intensively so there's movement, it's just not publicised," Malmgren said.
Sands had talks with Chinese Vice Trade Minister Long Yongtu in Beijing earlier this week, Kyodo said.
Malmgren predicted that the next 12 months would bring major progress on the issue. He was in Tokyo to attend informal discussions on China's entry into the world trade body.
Official talks on the issue are set for early November in Geneva, where the world trade body is headquartered.

U.S. and Chinese officials have been at odds for months over terms for China's WTO entry. Beijing has been seeking admission under more lenient standards set for developing nations, while Washington wants China to meet stricter standards that would take its huge economy into account.
But China's Long, in Tokyo for a seminar on China and the WTO, on Thursday painted a somewhat rosier picture of the potential for progress towards Beijing's joining the WTO.

"There used to be too much emphasis on the aspect that China needs the WTO, so the contracting parties could make any kind of request, which were sometimes not realistic and sometimes beyond the mandate of the WTO," he told Reuters.

"Now, I think the discussions have come to a more balanced view, that China's WTO membership also benefits other contracting parties and is especially important for strengthening the multilateral trade system," he said.
Long declined to comment on whether he felt Washington had altered its attitude but said China's position had not changed.

"China has not changed its attitude toward its membership in the WTO. The problem is, if members set the threshold of conditions too high, then China cannot afford it. We have to say 'no'. That's a matter of principle," he said.
Some Chinese officials worry that opening the market too quickly would do too much damage to China's loss-making state firms and protected industrial sectors.
